summary: Defines a canonical address format for LISP control messages and for lookup keys in the LISP mapping database, so many kinds of addresses can be carried in one encoding. It is experimental.

eli5.summary: Different kinds of addresses are put in one standard envelope so everyone can read them.

questions: how does lisp encode instance id
subtitle: A common envelope that lets LISP control messages carry addresses of many kinds, from AS numbers and MAC addresses to multicast groups and geo-coordinates.

tldr.problem: LISP control messages and mapping database lookups started out with only IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, but LISP needs to store and look up richer things such as instance IDs, AS numbers, locations and multicast entries.
tldr.mechanism: LCAF reserves one Address Family Identifier, 16387, and adds a small header with a Type field. The Type says how to read the payload that follows, and the payload can itself contain ordinary AFI-encoded addresses.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines Types 0 to 16, of which 11 are registered with IANA and the rest are unapproved experiments. It is an Experimental specification meant for cautious use in self-contained environments.

facts.label: Minimum size
facts.value: 8 bytes with the AFI, 6 bytes without

today: RFC 8060 is an Experimental RFC, and it has been updated by RFC 9306 and RFC 10040, so read those alongside it. The RFC itself says that as an Experimental specification the work is by definition incomplete.

sections.title: Why LISP Needs a Canonical Address Format
sections.content:
The Locator/ID Separation Protocol (RFC 6830) introduces two numbering spaces: Endpoint Identifiers (EIDs) and Routing Locators (RLOCs). An EID is the address a host uses, while an RLOC is the IPv4 or IPv6 address of an Egress Tunnel Router, and an EID maps to one or more RLOCs.

LISP control messages encode these values with a general syntax of Address Family Identifier (AFI), length and value. AFI 1 is IPv4 and AFI 2 is IPv6, using code points from the Address Family Numbers registry. This RFC describes those AFIs and introduces the LISP Canonical Address Format (LCAF), which can define LISP-specific encodings for arbitrary AFI values.

The RFC is upfront that, as an Experimental specification, the work is by definition incomplete. The Types are meant to support experimentation and cautious use in self-contained environments, and the detailed uses are left to separate use-case documents.
sections.eli5: Mail used to be addressed in only two ways. LCAF is a standard envelope that can hold many more kinds of addresses, plus a note saying what is inside.

sections.title: The LCAF Header
sections.content:
IANA assigned AFI value 16387 (0x4003) to LCAF. Every LISP Canonical Address starts with 6 bytes after that AFI: Rsvd1, Flags, Type, Rsvd2 and a 16-bit Length. A variable number of fields of variable length follows.

The reserved fields MUST be sent as 0 and ignored on receipt. Flags are for future use and are also zero on transmission and ignored on receipt. The 8-bit Type says how to read the rest. Length is in bytes and covers everything after the Length field. Including the AFI the smallest LCAF-encoded address is 8 bytes (Length of 0), and without the AFI it is 6 bytes.

Locator sets are sorted so that all routers see the same order. For an IP-address RLOC the sort key is the AFI and the address. When an RLOC is LCAF encoded, the key is the AFI and the LCAF Type, so a mix of AFI and LCAF records is ordered from smallest to largest AFI value.
sections.eli5: The front of the envelope has a stamp that says LCAF, a number saying what kind of thing is inside, and a number saying how long the contents are.

sections.title: The Approved Address Types
sections.content:
Section 4 defines the encodings for the initial set of approved Types. Many of them wrap an ordinary AFI-encoded address after their own fields, and many can encode either an EID or an RLOC.

  • Instance ID (Type 2) keeps overlapping private address spaces apart, for example when different organizations in a site use RFC 1918 addresses. It also supports segmented VPNs.
  • AS Number (Type 3) stores a 32-bit AS number for policy or documentation.
  • Geo-Coordinates (Type 5) carries latitude and longitude in degrees, minutes and seconds, plus altitude in meters, using the WGS 84 reference system.
  • NAT-Traversal (Type 7) carries the global and private ETR addresses, the Map-Server address and ports, and the RTR addresses. The Map-Server UDP port is set to 4342.
  • Multicast Info (Type 9) encodes an (Instance ID, S-prefix, G-prefix) entry, and Replication List Entry (Type 13) carries RTR or ETR locators with a level in the distribution tree.
  • Explicit Locator Path (Type 10) lists re-encapsulation hops, each with Lookup, RLOC-probe and Strict bits.
  • Security Key (Type 11) stores key material for a locator and can mark a key as revoked. Source/Dest Key (Type 12) is a 2-tuple lookup key.

AFI List (Type 1) packs several AFI-encoded values into one LCAF. The RFC uses it to bind IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, carry a MAC address (AFI 6) for Layer 2 VPNs, carry a DNS name or URI as an ASCII string (AFI 17), and nest another LCAF. A system should also use it as a compatibility mode when talking to peers that do not support a Type, so the receiver can still parse a locator address and skip the unknown part.
sections.eli5: There are different kinds of labelled envelopes: one for a private-network number, one for a map location, one for a group address, and so on. One special envelope can hold several smaller ones.

sections.title: Unapproved Experimental Types
sections.content:
Section 5 describes more encodings that are not registered with IANA. They are included to support further study of whether they work, whether there is demand, and what deployment problems they raise. They are restricted to cautious use in self-contained environments.

  • Application Data (Type 4) lets an ITR ask for a locator set for a specific application, using a TOS, traffic class or flow label, a protocol and local and remote port ranges.
  • Opaque Key (Type 6) is a generic lookup key split into fixed-width sub-fields, with a wildcard bitfield marking fields that are not used in the lookup.
  • Nonce Locator (Type 8) conveys a nonce for admission control at a public Proxy Egress Tunnel Router.
  • JSON Data Model (Type 14) carries JSON as text or binary, and Key/Value Address Pair (Type 15) attaches an address as an attribute of another address.
  • Encapsulation Format (Type 16) uses one bit per encapsulation an RLOC can accept: GUE, Geneve, NV-GRE, VXLAN-GPE, VXLAN, Layer 2 LISP and Layer 3 LISP.
sections.eli5: Some envelopes are still being tested in the lab. They are written down so people can try them out, but nobody should rely on them yet.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says the encodings are intended for their corresponding use cases and for self-contained environments, and that users should consider how the LISP-SEC threat model applies to their case.

The main concern is privacy. The Geo-Coordinates Type conveys physical location, which can be sensitive in unexpected ways, for example if the location is a router in a person's home. It should not be used unless needed, and the mapping system should be configured so geolocation is not returned gratuitously. The RFC also points to RFC 6280 (BCP 160) for location privacy and says future LISP work should look at threats beyond it.

The NAT-Traversal and Layer 2 MAC address encodings carry similar warnings: use policy controls so that the addresses are not abused.
sections.eli5: If an envelope says exactly where something is, a stranger could use that. So only put the location in when you really have to.

sections.title: The LCAF Types Registry
sections.content:
IANA created a registry named "LISP Canonical Address Format (LCAF) Types" for the 8-bit Type field. Future assignments use the Specification Required policy. The initial values registered by this document are 0 (Null Body), 1 (AFI List), 2 (Instance ID), 3 (AS Number), 5 (Geo-Coordinates), 7 (NAT-Traversal), 9 (Multicast Info), 10 (Explicit Locator Path), 11 (Security Key), 12 (Source/Dest Key) and 13 (Replication List Entry).

The unapproved Types 4, 6, 8, 14, 15 and 16 are not in that initial set.
sections.eli5: There is an official list of envelope labels. Eleven are on it already, and new ones can be added if someone writes down exactly how they work.
